subtitle: Creates lush, shimmering textures by blending your dry signal with modulated copies. From subtle thickening to dramatic ensemble effects.

introduction.title: What is Chorus?
introduction.text: Chorus creates the illusion of multiple instruments playing the same part by mixing your dry signal with one or more delayed copies that are modulated in pitch and timing. This mimics the natural variations that occur when multiple musicians play together: no two real performers ever play a unison part in perfectly identical pitch and timing, and it's exactly that small imperfection, recreated electronically, which makes a single guitar sound like it's been doubled rather than just processed. That's why chorus reads as a texture rather than an obvious effect at subtle settings, and why it can turn a single clean guitar into something that fills a mix the way a stack of overdubs would.

columns.title: How It Works
columns.text: A chorus pedal splits your signal into a dry path and one or more delayed copies, typically delayed by 15 to 35 milliseconds, short enough to be heard as one note rather than a discrete echo. A low-frequency oscillator (LFO) continuously speeds up and slows down that delay time, and because changing a delay's length also changes the effective pitch of the signal passing through it, the modulated copy drifts very slightly sharp and flat around the original pitch. Blending that drifting copy back with the dry signal is what creates the effect: the two signals reinforce each other at some frequencies and cancel at others as they move in and out of phase, producing the familiar swirling, watery texture. Adding more delay lines, each running its own LFO phase, thickens the effect further, which is how multi-voice and stereo choruses build a wider, more three-dimensional sound than a single-voice unit can.

columns.title: Musical Applications
columns.text: Because chorus works by adding pitch and timing variation, its most obvious use is thickening a single clean note or chord until it sounds doubled, which is why it became a standard way to fill space without actually recording a second guitar part. That mechanism is also behind its strong 80s association: pop and rock productions leaned on wide stereo chorus to make one guitar track occupy as much sonic space as a stack of overdubs. The same thickening works at a much lighter setting in jazz, fusion, and country playing, adding shimmer to clean or fingerpicked tone without drawing attention to itself, while on bass it fattens a thin low end in a mix before the pitch-smearing becomes audible as a distinct effect.

cards.title: Analog Chorus
cards.description: Analog chorus pedals create their delay using bucket-brigade device (BBD) chips, which pass the signal through a chain of capacitors that each hold and release it a fraction of a second later. That process has limited bandwidth and adds a small amount of noise and non-linearity along the way, and it's exactly those imperfections, rather than despite them, that give analog chorus its reputation for a warmer, more organic modulation than a digital circuit produces at equivalent settings.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Boss CE-1, MXR Analog Chorus, TC Electronic Corona

cards.title: Digital Chorus
cards.description: Digital chorus pedals generate the delay and modulation in the digital domain instead of through an analog BBD chain, which removes the bandwidth limits and noise floor that color an analog unit's tone. That precision is a trade-off rather than a straightforward upgrade: it lets a single pedal switch between several distinct chorus algorithms and expose far more parameters than an analog circuit can practically offer, though some players find the same precision makes the effect sound comparatively sterile next to an analog pedal's built-in imperfections.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Boss CH-1, Strymon Mobius, Eventide TimeFactor

cards.title: Stereo Chorus
cards.description: A stereo chorus sends the dry signal to one output and the modulated copy to the other, so instead of blending both signals into a single channel they arrive at the listener's left and right ears separately. That physical separation creates a genuine sense of width that a mono chorus can only approximate through phase cancellation, which is why the deep, wide chorus sound closely associated with classic 80s guitar tone really requires two amps or a stereo signal path to hear in full, not just the pedal on its own.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Boss CE-5, Roland JC-120 amp, rack processors

cards.title: Multi-Voice Chorus
cards.description: A multi-voice chorus runs several delay lines at once, each with its own LFO rate and phase, rather than modulating a single copy of the signal. Layering that many independently drifting copies together is closer to what actually happens when a group of instruments or voices play the same part, none perfectly in tune or time with one another, which is why these units are described as producing an ensemble effect rather than a single-voice thickening.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: EHX Small Clone, Boss CE-20, vintage string machines

fields.label: Rate/Speed
fields.value: LFO frequency (how fast the modulation cycles)

fields.label: Depth/Intensity
fields.value: Amount of pitch modulation

fields.label: Level/Mix
fields.value: Balance between dry and effected signal

fields.label: Tone/EQ
fields.value: Frequency shaping of the effect

fields.label: Delay Time
fields.value: Base delay before modulation

fields.label: Feedback
fields.value: Amount of processed signal fed back

fields.label: Phase
fields.value: Relationship between multiple voices

fields.label: Waveform
fields.value: Shape of the modulating LFO

cards.title: Boss CE-1 Chorus Ensemble
cards.description: Boss built the CE-1 in 1976 by taking the chorus/vibrato circuit already used in Roland's JC-120 Jazz Chorus amplifier and housing it in a standalone floor pedal, making it both the first pedal Boss ever released and the first chorus pedal sold as a discrete effect. Its two-mode design, a subtle blended chorus and a more dramatic pitch-only vibrato, combined with the warmth and noise inherent to its BBD circuit, set a template that most analog chorus pedals since have tried to recreate.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Warm, analog modulation with rich harmonic content and smooth transitions

fields.label: Notable Users
fields.value: Andy Summers (The Police), John Frusciante (Red Hot Chili Peppers)

cards.title: Electro-Harmonix Small Clone
cards.description: The Small Clone pares chorus down to two knobs, rate and depth, plus a switch for a wider "deep" modulation, which makes it fast to dial in without a large control set to navigate. Kurt Cobain's use of one on Nirvana's "Come As You Are" gave it mainstream visibility that its low price and simplicity wouldn't have earned on their own, and that same directness has kept it a favorite with clean-tone players who want an obvious, unmistakably analog chorus without wading through menus or extra parameters.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Rich, deep chorus with a slightly dark character and smooth modulation

fields.label: Notable Users
fields.value: Kurt Cobain (Nirvana)

cards.title: Boss CE-5 Chorus Ensemble
cards.description: The CE-5 pairs true stereo outputs with a switchable EQ voicing that cuts some of the high-frequency content chorus can add, which matters because that top-end shimmer that sounds pleasant through headphones can turn brittle and thin once it's pushed through a PA. Between the EQ options and the stereo spread, it can get closer to a two-amp analog chorus rig's sense of space out of a single compact pedal.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Clean, precise digital chorus with wide stereo imaging and flexible control

cards.title: TC Electronic Corona Chorus
cards.description: The Corona runs on TC Electronic's TonePrint platform, which lets players load a custom or artist-designed modulation setting into the pedal from a phone app rather than being limited to what the physical knobs can dial in, and switch between several distinct chorus voicings, including emulations of classic analog circuits, from one small enclosure. That flexibility is the trade-off against an all-analog pedal: fewer inherent sonic quirks of its own, but access to a much wider range of chorus characters without needing several dedicated pedals.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Versatile digital chorus with multiple classic and modern algorithms

cards.title: 80s Pop & Rock
cards.description: Chorus became the signature guitar sound of 80s pop and rock largely because of what a wide stereo setting does to a clean tone: it turns a single note into something that sounds like it's filling a large room by itself. Pairing it with reverb pushed that further, since the reverb's diffuse tail reinforced the space the chorus had already created, letting one guitarist's clean tone carry as much sonic weight in a mix as a much busier arrangement.

fields.label: Settings
fields.value: Deep, slow rate, stereo spread

fields.label: Artists
fields.value: The Police, The Cure, U2

cards.title: Jazz & Fusion
cards.description: Jazz and fusion players tend to keep chorus subtle enough that it isn't consciously heard as an effect: a small amount of pitch modulation adds depth and movement to a clean tone that would otherwise sound comparatively flat through a PA or recording. Pushing the depth or rate further starts to compete with the harmonic complexity of jazz voicings, which is why the style favors restraint over the dramatic wide settings used in pop and rock.

fields.label: Settings
fields.value: Subtle depth, medium rate

fields.label: Artists
fields.value: John Scofield, Pat Metheny, Bill Frisell

cards.title: Country & Folk
cards.description: A light chorus setting brings out high-frequency detail in fingerpicked and clean electric parts by very slightly doubling and detuning the signal, which reads as added sparkle rather than an obvious effect. Because country and folk playing relies on note-to-note clarity to carry the arrangement, players in these styles typically keep the depth low enough that the pitch modulation stays below the threshold of being consciously noticed.

fields.label: Settings
fields.value: Light depth, faster rate

fields.label: Artists
fields.value: Brad Paisley, Keith Urban, many session players

cards.title: Alternative & Indie
cards.description: Alternative and indie guitarists use chorus across its full range, from a light thickening on a clean tone to deep, slow modulation that all but obscures the note's original pitch. At its most extreme, deep and slow chorus stops sounding like a doubled guitar and starts sounding like a wash of texture, which is the effect bands built around dreamy, atmospheric arrangements have leaned on to blur the line between a guitar part and an ambient backdrop.

fields.label: Settings
fields.value: Various, often deep and slow

fields.label: Artists
fields.value: Nirvana, My Bloody Valentine, Radiohead

cards.title: Best Practices
cards.description: Chorus is easy to overdo because its effect compounds with whatever other modulated or delayed effects are already in your chain: a setting that sounds tasteful on its own can turn to mush once it's stacked with delay and reverb in a full mix. Starting subtle and only adding depth if the mix still calls for it keeps the effect adding dimension rather than smearing the pitch definition of your playing.

cards.title: Signal Chain Position
cards.description: Chorus generally sits after gain-based effects like distortion and overdrive, because modulating an already-distorted signal accentuates the pitch wobble in a way that can sound unpleasantly warbly, while modulating a clean or lightly overdriven signal keeps it smooth. Placing it before time-based effects like delay and reverb means those effects repeat or diffuse the already-modulated signal, which generally produces a more cohesive, spacious sound than the reverse order.

sections.title: Chorus Settings Guide
sections.warningText: Chorus sounds different at various volumes and in different rooms. What sounds perfect at bedroom levels might be too much in a band mix. Always adjust for the musical context.
